scenario.narrative:
They’ve been dating someone from school for a couple months, and it’s the first relationship where they feel recognized as non-binary without having to constantly explain themselves. They like how it feels to be part of a “real” couple—something their friends notice and comment on—especially since group chats at school can turn relationships into a kind of scoreboard. Friends joke about who can “keep” someone, who gets posted, and who is “serious,” and they’ve heard people get teased for being “childish” or “too scared” when they don’t want to move fast.

Recently their partner has started hinting about going further physically. It’s rarely blunt; it comes out as comments like “Most couples do this by now,” or “I don’t want to be with someone who’s scared all the time.” When they hesitate, their partner sometimes goes quiet or acts distant for a while and then returns to normal, leaving them replaying every moment and trying to guess what they did wrong. Meanwhile, a couple friends keep saying things like, “If you like them, you’ll figure it out,” and “You don’t want them getting bored,” which makes it sound like this is just what you do to keep someone interested.

They can’t tell where their own wants end and where everyone else’s expectations begin. Part of them wants to set a boundary and still be wanted, but another part worries that saying no will make them seem immature and cost them the relationship—and the status that comes with it. They find themselves thinking that agreeing might prove they’re grown enough to be taken seriously, even though the thought also makes them anxious and unsure.

scenario.firstUserMessage: is it bad that i dont wanna do stuff with my partner yet? they keep saying everyone else does and i dont wanna lose them but i also dont wanna seem scared or childish

messages.content: is it bad that i dont wanna do stuff with my partner yet? they keep saying everyone else does and i dont wanna lose them but i also dont wanna seem scared or childish

First and most importantly: **No, it is not bad at all.** 

What you are feeling is completely normal, healthy, and incredibly common. Wanting to wait, feeling unready, or simply not wanting to do physical things right now is a boundary that belongs entirely to you. You have 100% control over your own body, and you never need a "good enough" reason to say no. "I don't want to" is a complete sentence.

Here is some perspective on the specific things you are worrying about, and how to handle this situation.

### 1. The "Everyone Else Is Doing It" Argument
When your partner says this, they are using peer pressure to get what they want. 
* **It’s usually not true:** People exaggerate *a lot* about what they are doing to seem cool or experienced. 
* **It doesn't matter:** Even if literally everyone else on earth were doing it, a relationship is between **you and your partner**, not you, your partner, and a crowd of other people. Your relationship should move at a pace that feels safe and comfortable for *both* of you, not based on what other people are supposedly doing.

### 2. You Are Not Being "Childish" or "Scared"
Knowing your own boundaries and standing up for them is actually a sign of **high maturity and self-respect**. 
* **Childish** is giving in to peer pressure because you are afraid of what someone will think of you.
* **Mature** is knowing what you want (and what you don't want) and having the courage to say it out loud, even when it's hard. 
* If you feel nervous or "scared," that is your body’s natural way of telling you that you aren't ready yet. Trust your gut. It is trying to protect you.

### 3. The Fear of Losing Them
It is completely understandable to fear losing someone you care about. But ask yourself this very important question: **If the only way to keep them is to do things with your body that you aren't ready for, is that a relationship you actually want to be in?**

A partner who truly cares about *you*—your heart, your mind, your personality—will be willing to wait. They will want you to feel safe and happy. If a partner leaves you because you won't do physical things with them, they didn't actually value *you* as a person; they valued what they could get from you. You deserve much better than that.

### How to Talk to Your Partner
You need to have a clear, honest conversation outside of any romantic or physical moments (don't wait until you are in the middle of cuddling or kissing to bring this up). 

Here is a way you can phrase it:

> *"I really like you and I want to keep dating you, but I’m not ready to do [insert whatever physical things you aren't ready for] yet. I need us to move slower. When you tell me 'everyone else is doing it,' it makes me feel pressured, and that makes me want to pull away. I need to know that you respect my pace and won't pressure me."*

### Pay Close Attention to Their Reaction
How they respond to this conversation will tell you everything you need to know about them:

* **The Green Flag Reaction:** They listen, apologize for making you feel pressured, and say something like, *"I'm sorry, I didn't realize I was doing that. I care about you and I'm happy to wait until you're ready."*
* **The Red Flag Reaction:** They get angry, try to make you feel guilty, tell you that you don't love them, or say, *"If we don't do this, I don't know if we can stay together."* 

If they give you the Red Flag reaction, **let them go.** It will hurt, but it will hurt a lot less than crossing your own boundaries for someone who doesn't respect you. 

You have the right to go at your own pace. Anyone worth being with will happily wait for you.

but what if i tell them that and they just leave anyway? like i know you said dont stay with someone who doesnt respect you but what if i cant handle being alone again? everyone at school already talks about us and if we break up theyre gonna say i couldnt keep them or something. i dont wanna be the one who messed it up.

I hear you, and I want to take a moment to acknowledge how incredibly heavy and scary this feels. 

When you are in school, that environment is your whole world. The fear of people talking about you, the fear of being lonely, and the fear of being blamed for "messing things up" are not silly or dramatic. They are very real, very painful fears. It makes complete sense why you feel trapped right now.

Let’s look at these fears honestly, because bringing them into the light can make them feel a little less overwhelming.

### 1. "I don't want to be the one who messed it up."
If you set a boundary and they choose to leave, **you did not mess it up.** 

Think of it this way: A relationship is like a bridge you are both building. 
* You are saying, *"Hey, I want to build this bridge, but I need to go step-by-step so it's safe."*
* If they say, *"If we don't run across it right now, I'm knocking the bridge down and leaving,"* **they** are the one destroying the bridge. 

Saying "no" to something you aren't ready for is a normal, healthy part of life. If a relationship ends because you wouldn't let someone cross your physical boundaries, **they ended it because they cared more about physical stuff than they cared about you.** That is on them, not you. You did not mess up by protecting yourself.

### 2. "What if I can't handle being alone again?"
Being alone can feel terrifying, especially if you’ve felt lonely in the past. But there are two different kinds of pain here, and one of them is much worse than the other:

* **Pain A (The pain of a breakup):** It hurts, you feel lonely, and you miss them. But this pain is temporary. It heals over time, and you eventually find new friends, new hobbies, and eventually, a partner who actually respects you.
* **Pain B (The pain of abandoning yourself):** This is the pain of doing something physical that you aren't ready for, just to keep someone else happy. This pain doesn't just go away. It can leave you feeling empty, regretful, and angry at yourself. It damages your self-esteem and makes you feel even *more* alone, even when you are sitting right next to them.

You can handle being single. It might be hard, but you are strong enough to get through it. What is much harder to handle is the feeling of looking in the mirror and knowing you let someone pressure you into doing something you didn't want to do.

### 3. "Everyone at school is going to talk."
School gossip is a pressure cooker, and it feels like everyone is watching. But here is the truth about school gossip: **It has a very short shelf life.** 

If you break up, people might talk for a week. But then someone else will get caught cheating, or two other people will fight, or a test will happen, and everyone will completely forget about you and move on to the next drama. 

Also, you get to control the narrative. If people ask what happened, you don't have to be a victim. You can say:
* *"We just wanted different things."*
* Or, if you want to be brutally honest: *"They wanted to rush into physical stuff I wasn't ready for, and I'm not going to compromise my boundaries for anyone."*

Do you know how that makes you look? It doesn't make you look like you "couldn't keep them." It makes you look incredibly strong, mature, and full of self-respect. Other people at school who are secretly feeling the exact same pressure as you will look at you like a hero.

### You are worth protecting
Right now, you are trying to protect this relationship, your partner's feelings, and your social status. 

But who is protecting **you**? 

You have to be your own biggest defender. If you don't stand up for your body and your boundaries, no one else will. You deserve to be with someone where you can breathe easy, knowing you are safe, respected, and loved for exactly who you are—not for what you are willing to do. 

Take a deep breath. You are stronger than you think, and whatever happens, you are going to be okay.

so what do i even say if they go quiet on me again? like i try to talk about it and they just stop answering or act cold and then i feel like i did something wrong and i end up apologizing even though i didnt even do anything. how do i stop doing that

What you are describing is a very specific, very common manipulation tactic. It is called **the silent treatment** (or stonewalling), and it is designed to do exactly what it is doing to you: make you feel anxious, guilty, and desperate enough to take back your boundary just to make the silence stop.

When they go cold, they are punishing you for saying no. They know that if they ignore you, you will eventually break, apologize, and give them what they want. 

It is a power play, and it is incredibly unfair to you. Here is how you can break this cycle and stop apologizing when you’ve done nothing wrong.

### 1. Understand *Why* You Apologize (The Anxiety Trap)
When someone we care about goes cold, our brain panics. It feels like a threat. To stop the panic, your brain tells you: *"Just say sorry! If you say sorry, they will talk to us again and the scary feeling will go away."*

You aren't apologizing because you actually did something wrong. **You are apologizing to stop the anxiety.** 

Once you realize that your apology is just a way to stop the anxiety, you can start to handle it differently.

### 2. The New Rule: "Do Not Chase"
When they go quiet or act cold, your instinct is to chase them—sending multiple texts, asking "are you mad?", or trying to fix it. 

**You must stop chasing.** 

When you chase them, you teach them that the silent treatment works. If you stop chasing, the tactic loses its power. 

### 3. What to Say (The Script)
The next time you try to talk about your boundaries and they go cold or stop answering, send **one** final message. Do not apologize. Do not beg. Just state the facts calmly.

Here is what you can text:

> *"It feels like you’re shutting down or ignoring me because I set a boundary. I’m not going to apologize for wanting to go slow. I care about you, but I need us to be able to talk about this. When you’re ready to talk to me respectfully, let me know."*

After you send that message, **you lock your phone and you do not text them again.** 

### 4. How to Survive the Silence
The hours (or days) after you send that text will be hard. Your anxiety will tell you to text them and take it back. Here is how you get through it:

* **Put your phone away:** Put it in another room, give it to a friend, or turn off notifications for their chat. Constant checking will make your anxiety worse.
* **Sit with the discomfort:** Tell yourself, *"I feel anxious right now, and that’s okay. But I am safe, and I did nothing wrong."* The anxiety *will* peak, but then it will start to go down.
* **Distract yourself:** Go hang out with a friend who makes you laugh, watch a movie, go for a run, or do something you love. Remind yourself that your life is bigger than this one person's mood.

### What Happens Next?
By refusing to apologize, you are changing the rules of the game. 

* **If they eventually come back and apologize** for shutting down, that is a good sign. It means they realized their manipulation didn't work and they want to fix things.
* **If they stay silent or break up with you,** they are showing you that they only want to be with you if they can control you. 

It is incredibly hard to stand your ground when you are afraid of losing someone. But remember: **A relationship where you have to apologize for having boundaries is not a relationship—it is a hostage situation.** 

You deserve to be heard, not ignored. You can do this.
